analysis.one_liner: Requires car makers to share repair and diagnostic information with owners and independent repair shops.
analysis.headline: The bill, introduced with bipartisan support from 12 senators, never received a hearing or vote in the Senate Commerce Committee and died when the 108th Congress ended in January 2005.
analysis.plain_summary: Modern cars are run by computers, and manufacturers were increasingly keeping the diagnostic codes and repair information needed to fix them exclusive to franchised dealers. This bill would have required car makers to give owners and independent repair shops the information needed to diagnose, service, and repair their vehicles, with the Federal Trade Commission writing the rules and owners or repair shops able to sue over violations. Car makers would keep genuine trade secrets but could not withhold information they already gave their own dealers.
analysis.who_benefits: Vehicle owners, who could choose between a dealer and any independent shop and could shop around on price; independent repair shops and the auto parts industry, which gained access to the same repair information dealers had; and used-car owners in particular, since older vehicles are often repaired outside dealerships.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Car owners and independent repair shops

how_it_helps.text: Manufacturers must promptly provide owners, repair facilities, and the FTC the information needed to diagnose, service, or repair a vehicle, including information to integrate replacement equipment [S3].
Information cannot be withheld if it has already been provided to franchised dealers or other repair facilities, closing the gap that let dealers fix cars independent shops could not [S3].
Vehicle owners and repair facilities can sue in federal court to stop violations and recover litigation costs, without regard to the amount in controversy or the parties' citizenship [S3].
The bill's findings cite the aftermarket parts industry's 5 million workers and note that restricted repair information limits consumer choice and competition [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Car manufacturers, who would lose their exclusive grip on repair and diagnostic information, and their franchised dealers, who would face more competition for service work from independent shops and aftermarket parts makers.

drawbacks.text: The bill carves out genuine trade secrets: the FTC cannot force public disclosure of information entitled to trade secret protection, which manufacturers could have tested in contested proceedings [S3].

FTC rules would only take effect for vehicles manufactured after model year 1994 and would be barred from interfering with the EPA's authority over emissions diagnostics systems, limiting the bill's scope [S3].

Manufacturers argued at the time that forcing disclosure of proprietary diagnostic and technical information risked exposing intellectual property and that their dealer networks already provided safe, reliable repair; the bill required FTC rulemaking with trade-secret hearings that could delay relief (general policy knowledge; the trade-secret and hearing provisions are in [S3]).

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The consumer benefit is straightforward: a working car is a necessity, and repair costs are a regular hit to household budgets. Restricting who can fix a car and what parts can be used raises those costs. The trade-secret carve-out, the model-year limitation, and the EPA carve-out were real limits, but the core mechanism — requiring manufacturers to share with independents the same information dealers get — is a direct fix for an information monopoly. The main cost falls on manufacturers and dealers, not on the public.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced in February 2004, referred to the Senate Commerce Committee, and the committee never took it up, so it died when the 108th Congress ended in January 2005.

narrative.text: Senator Lindsey Graham introduced the bill on February 26, 2004, and it was read twice and referred to the Committee on Commerce, Science, and Transportation [S5].
Eleven senators cosponsored, 9 Democrats and 2 Republicans, giving the bill bipartisan support [S4].
The action history shows no hearing, no markup, no committee vote, and no floor action after the referral [S5].
The 108th Congress ended on January 3, 2005, and the bill was not reintroduced into that Congress's remaining calendar, leaving no vote ever taken on the merits [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Car manufacturers and their dealer networks kept exclusive control of repair and diagnostic information; owners and independent shops continued paying dealer-only prices for some repairs. The fight resurfaced in later Congresses and industry eventually agreed to voluntary disclosure commitments rather than a law.

for.name: Sen. Lindsey Graham
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Motor Vehicle Owners' Right to Repair Act and referred it to the Commerce Committee.

against.name: Senate Committee on Commerce, Science, and Transportation
against.what_they_did: Never held a hearing, markup, or vote; the bill sat in committee until the Congress ended.

against.name: Alliance of Automobile Manufacturers and major car makers
against.what_they_did: Campaigned against federal right-to-repair legislation, arguing dealer networks already provided safe and reliable repair and that proprietary information should be protected.

against.name: Auto aftermarket and repair advocacy groups
against.role: Independent repair and parts industry coalition
against.what_they_did: Pushed publicly for passage in the Senate and House, keeping the issue alive across multiple Congresses after this bill died.

sides.party_line_note: The sponsor was a Republican and 9 of the 11 cosponsors were Democrats, so support crossed party lines; no vote record exists because the committee never acted.

industries.note: Manufacturers were increasingly restricting diagnostic codes and repair data to their own dealers; the bill would have required sharing that information with owners and independent shops. Their gain from the status quo was higher dealer-controlled service and parts revenue, which comes at owners' expense.
Dealers' service departments would have faced more competition from independent shops able to fix the same vehicles, putting pressure on service profit margins.

industries.industry: Independent repair shops and the auto aftermarket parts industry
industries.note: The bill gave shops access to the same repair information dealers had, letting them compete for work they sometimes could not perform. The bill's findings note the aftermarket supports over 5 million workers and $200 billion in annual sales [S3].
Owners could choose where to repair their cars and between original and aftermarket parts, with competition expected to lower repair costs.
